utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom and also to those who are assisting us just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Before we continue the examination of Mr. Babic, the Chamber confirms reception of a letter dated the 4th of June, 2004, although we have read it in 30 seconds, the Chamber will consider during the next break whether it will deal with the matter at this very moment or not. We still have to spend more time on it. Then the Chamber has received the Defence motion to postpone the cross-examination of Milan Babic until after his sentencing, a very short motion, which, as far as the arguments are concerned, refers to the submissions made in respect of the testimony of Mr. Deronjic. The relief sought is first of all the cross-examination of the Prosecution witness would be postponed until after his sentencing, and a second relief sought is the Defence seeks to make oral submissions on this matter. The Chamber has deliberated first of all on the second relief sought this morning and the Defence is granted ten minutes to further elaborate on it. The Chamber has kept in mind that, first of all, the contents of the motion in respect of Mr. Deronjic and the argument exchanged, also the decision taken in this respect, the Chamber notes that the motion does not submit any difference between the -- I would say the Deronjic situation and the present situation with Mr. Babic. The Chamber also noted that where, in Deronjic, it was the testimony to be postponed, here it is just cross-examination, and the motion has been filed after the examination-in-chief of Mr. Babic had started. The Chamber, therefore, gives ten minutes to the Defence to orally make further submissions into the matter, and the Chamber expects the Defence to not introduce new elements but, rather, elaborate on what is in the motion at this moment. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, thank you very much for that opportunity. When Your Honour asked me not to introduce new elements, on the other hand, I assume that Your Honour wishes me to say something new rather than simply repeat what's been said before, otherwise there's not much value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Use your ten minutes as you deem fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. So far as the differences between -- I won't repeat any of what I -- we said in relation to Mr. Deronjic. Your Honours have that, but it is there. So far as the differences between the situation of Mr. Babic and Mr. Deronjic are concerned, first of all, the point that we are only seeking to postpone cross-examination. The reason we are only seeking to postpone cross-examination in relation to Mr. Babic is because we have already had the examination-in-chief. So we can't postpone that any more. That really goes back to a different question, which is why we did not bring this application before in relation to Mr. Babic. Therefore, covering both examination-in-chief and cross-examination. There are two reasons for that. One is a simple practical one, which is, even though the motion is very short, that's not the primary reason. We have been absolutely overwhelmed with things to do. But that's not really essentially the reason. The point is this, Your Honour: We -- the situation has kept changing this week. We -- in effect, we have been trying to understand and see from the bits of information which have been made available to the Defence, in effect, I'll put it bluntly, Your Honour, what is going on. We have been -- as we've indicated before, we and Mr. Krajisnik as well, we have been extremely puzzled as to exactly why events have been happening in a particular sequence, why a particular hearing in another case is listed for hearing, announced to be taking place one day, then the next day or even the same day I believe sometimes it's announced that the previous statements was inoperative and it's all going to be different. We've been very, very puzzled by that. We now simply, on the basis of the submissions we made in relation to Mr. Deronjic, on the Defence side, we no longer see that there is any good reason whatever for Mr. Babic's evidence to be heard before he is sentenced. And we simply reiterate our submissions in the Deronjic case to this extent: That our submission was there that unless there is some significant practical obstacle to having a sensitive witness, sensitive in relation to the content of this case, giving his evidence when he is freed of any possible incentive in relation to his imminent sentencing, then that opportunity should be taken. The fact that it cannot be taken in relation to examination-in-chief is in a sense not quite so serious, because, after all, the whole point of cross-examination is that a witness can qualify, withdraw, modify, anything at all that he has said in examination-in-chief under cross-examination, because it's not until he has completed his evidence that that is his evidence. So most of what is achieved by -- I wouldn't go so far as to say all, but a very great part of what is achieved by deferring a witness's evidence so that he is relieved of any possible incentive in relation to the question of sentencing is achieved if that happens certainly before the beginning of his cross-examination, and to some extent it's achieved if he is able to complete his evidence at all after he is sentenced. In the present circumstances, it seemed, for example, that in the light of announcements made in the last 48 hours, I think it is, Your Honour, that there wasn't, in fact, any significant practical obstacle to Mr. Babic's sentencing taking place soon. It was announced yet again on the 2nd of June, which is two days ago, it was announced by a spokesman for the Tribunal that Mr. Babic's sentencing would take place on Monday morning. That was withdrawn I think later the same day. But in the light of the comments that Your Honour made and the explanation that Your Honour very kindly gave to us earlier this week as to what the practical difficulties were in relation to that scheduling, it seemed that against those comments, that the position in the other case, and of course the thing is when I'm addressing this Trial Chamber, that is another case, that that other Trial Chamber, which of course is in fact Your Honours, the three of you, but that other Trial Chamber apparently was in a position and there was no difficulty about Mr. Babic's sentencing taking place soon. We do understand, and we have always respected and, with respect to, supported the practical questions in relation to the immediate scheduling, for example, on Tuesday. We understand that fully and we don't create any difficulty or objection or suggestion that there's anything wrong about that. That's perfectly natural, reasonable. However, it is apparent that there isn't, and in effect never has been, any serious question of any long deferral in relation to the sentencing of Mr. Babic. We have also become significantly troubled by what is emerged in the last couple of days in this court in relation to possibilities of refusal on the part of Mr. Babic to give evidence. The Court expressed strong opposition, in effect, if I may put it that way, but there was strong dissatisfaction with the notion that any witness might say that he might refuse to give evidence on an occasion yesterday. The Court didn't make any such comment earlier when it was indicated that Mr. Babic might in slightly different circumstances simply refuse to continue with his evidence. The fact that on two occasions now we have had suggestions that Mr. Babic might in some circumstances refuse to give evidence does add to the Defence's concerns as to the position of Mr. Babic as compared to Mr. Deronjic. And one of the things that we would distinctly ask to know is whether there is, in fact, any concern at all on the Prosecution's part or the Trial Chamber's part that if Mr. Babic is sentenced, that he will not then willingly return to give evidence. Because it must be a simple fact whether the Prosecution have that concern or not, and whether the Trial Chamber have that concern or not. Because if that concern is there at all, then we submit the Defence should know that there is that concern. Because that is a highly relevant factor, because the very fact that there is that concern itself indicates the reasons why it is dangerous for a witness in Mr. Babic's position to complete his evidence and have it finalised, subject -- he can always be recalled, of course. The Trial Chamber always has that discretion. But on the face of it, have his evidence completed before he is sentenced. If there is that concern, it has a strong tendency to reinforce at the very objection which was made on the Deronjic motion, which is repeated here, and it becomes stronger. So we do certainly ask to know that concern. If we are told that, frankly, by the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber, of course we would respect frankness. I don't mean any disrespect there. But if we are told that is no part of anybody's concern, at least that eliminates one element from the whole consideration. It doesn't remove at the basic point that when in relation to such -- an apparently important witness, we'll all make or submissions in due course when his evidence is completed, as to how important his evidence is. But it's quite plain that the nature of the topic and the nature of his evidence and the way that Mr. Babic has approached it, it's quite plain that he is regarded by the Prosecution as a significant element of the case against Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I remind you that there's one minute left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I said I would keep to the ten minutes and I will keep to the ten minutes and in fact may I offer Your Honours 45 seconds as a present from the Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any need to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps simply, Your Honours, to note the Prosecutor's submission that the various factors raised by Mr. Stewart do not meaningfully distinguish this matter from the relevant circumstances of the Deronjic case, and in fact the belated filing of this motion, underlines the reason for a meaningful distinction between those two circumstances if the practice followed in the Deronjic situation and that should be completed here is to -- if we're to deviate from that. So I don't think sufficient distinctions have been drawn, and there's no basis for this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. The Chamber will withdraw. We have deliberated this morning on the motion before, having heard the further submissions of the parties. But you would not be surprised if we speculated on what we might hear, so therefore, it might not take that much time to reach a decision. We'll withdraw and the parties are instructed to remain available to restart soon. --- Break taken at 9.22 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will give an oral ruling on the motion filed by the Defence yesterday. The motion, as far as the relief sought under number 1, is denied. A decision will follow, giving, in writing, the reasons for the rejection of the motion. The Chamber makes, nevertheless, a few observations in respect of it. First of all, the Chamber expects the Chamber in the Babic case, and this Chamber can know, to give its judgement on the exclusive basis of the material presented to it in that case, and hearings have been closed. That's the first observation. The second observation is that the matters pointed at by the Defence, which raised some questions that these matters were considered by the Chamber, and the Chamber is in a position to establish that there is not a relation between those questions and concerns which would cause and would justify the delay of the cross-examination of Mr. Babic. The third observation is that the Chamber has considered the relatively late filing, and the reasons given for it by the Defence, when reaching its decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is the decision and the observations. The written decision will follow. And we'll now continue the hearing of evidence. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to start cross-examining Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. I do have a couple of -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just a couple of observations to make before Mr. Babic comes into court. I'm grateful for assurances contained in what Your Honour has just said. In return, I would also like to offer this assurance as to -- the Trial Chamber please understands that the filing of the motion was not related or motivated in any way by a simple wish to defer cross-examination of Mr. Babic for practical reasons. We would make those submissions frankly and independently, and will if necessary make them independently in relation to lack of preparation and so on. That was not part of the motivation in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Mr. Stewart, that the Chamber doesn't need this assurance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that, Your Honour. I do appreciate that very much. Your Honour, the other matter is a practical point which is that -- that was a practical point. It's a point related to Mr. Babic's testimony. We -- after the exchange yesterday and the decision in relation to 92 bis, we just reminded ourselves on the Defence side that at various points in his written statement, which is in evidence, Mr. Babic says -- I'll just pick a random example, really. It's in the last paragraph, paragraph 15. "I spoke in my testimony in the Milosevic trial about Mladic", and in the previous paragraph, "I spoke in my testimony in Milosevic". We understand the position to be that although his statement referred to that, those bits of his Milosevic trial testimony which are not in, that in effect, those phrases in his statement should in effect be excised and treated as not there because he's given his evidence orally on the matters which Mr. Tieger explored with him and the particular limited number of pages are in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber understands the position to be that if he says: "I testified about these issues in the Milosevic trial", that since those portions are not tendered and not in evidence, that it's limited to the mere fact that he testified on these issues in the Milosevic trial, whatever the relevance of that would be. So if you would contest that, you could limited yourself to say: Did you testify on those issues? Or we put it to you that you did not testify on those issues. And then he could say, for example: I did that on pages so-and-so and so. Because that's what remains in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- with respect, what Your Honour has just said a hundred per cent reflects our understanding, but we wanted it confirm. I can also assure Your Honour that the likelihood of time being spent in cross-examination by my challenging Mr. Babic as to whether he did talk about a particular topic in the Milosevic trial is about 0 per cent. So we wish to assure you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I did not give you an opportunity to respond to it, but it seems clear to me that at least the Chamber, by reducing the 1.100 pages to 6, that means that the rest is not in evidence. So the only meaning of such -- of those parts of the statement is that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. There was no need for the Prosecution to respond, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I simply then also -- sorry. Just turning on my microphone just to say thank you for that, Your Honour. Simply to say this, yes, in answer to Your Honour's question, yes, I am ready to proceed with cross-examination of Mr. Babic. I do simply want to say this, though, Your Honour, first: I'm not ready in the sense of what I regard as normal, satisfactory state of preparation and readiness to examine a witness. In my and -- well, really the whole of my team's professional judgement, we are not in that adequate state of readiness. But I did say to the Tribunal that I would begin Mr. Babic's cross-examination this morning. I did say that we would do our very best professionally to be ready to do that. We have complied with one of those. We are about to comply with the other of those. We will meet our assurances and undertakings. It was expressly mentioned Your Honour, and the bridge that we have to cross -- if at any point I do feel that I simply ought not, in fairness to Mr. Krajisnik, to simply continue without any observation or contesting of that position, then, Your Honour, it will be my professional duty to say so, and I will say so. And then we -- that is a bridge that when we come to it, if we come to it, the Trial Chamber then no doubt will cross hand in hand with all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether there are any bridges on the road, we'll hear that from you and we'll see that. Then the security is invited to accompany Mr. Babic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic. We had some procedural issues, so that kept you waiting for 50 minutes. Mr. Babic, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. I would like to add to that that, since, of course, this Chamber and the Prosecution and the Defence and yourself are aware of your present position where you have been found guilty in your own case and that you're still awaiting sentencing, that the solemn declaration is the only basis on which you should answer questions put to you, especially since you're now beginning to answer questions by the Defence. I just wanted to remind you that this is what is expected from you as a witness. I hope you do understand that and that it's of -- it would not even be of any use to do anything else. Is that understood, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'm going to ask you quite frequently about parts of your evidence that you have already given over the last couple of days in this trial, and I will refer from time to time specifically to passages of evidence. On the whole, they will be short passages. I don't believe you will have any real difficulty, Mr. Babic, in understanding and following what I'm putting to you by way of what it is you've already said. If, of course, you find at any time, well, it's difficult to absorb what I'm saying without seeing in front of you what you have said, and that will have to be interpreted for you, I think, then please inform the Trial Chamber, and generally, of course, if at any time my questions to you are not clear, then I wish you to -- not to try to answer them while they're not clear, but to ask specifically for them to be clarified, because that does sometimes happen. But I will, as the phrase goes, do my best. Mr. Babic, you -- I'm also going to refer to some passages in the statement, which is part of your evidence that you made on various dates, most recently in March of this year. In your statement, and also in your evidence -- and this is at page 26, for everybody else's record, pages 26 and 27 of yesterday's -- it's at the moment the uncorrected transcript. Of course, that's what we have available currently. You -- in fact, it goes on to page 27, the particular point. You said this, and I'll just quote you your statement. It's a short passage, paragraph 11. You say the "misuse of history went further than World War II. Many of the Bosnian Serb leaders referred to Muslims as Turks. This expression was used in Bosnia. This is a term that goes farther than the simple derogatory sense and expresses a hostility rooted in history." The -- you just mentioned this, really, in your evidence, oral evidence, and I don't believe that what you said really added anything to that. Do you suggest, first of all, that this is a term that is ever used by Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke generally about that. I do not remember Mr. Krajisnik using that term. But I spoke in a general sense. A lot of people used that term. A lot of people from the leadership of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Such as who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, I could hear it from Dr. Vukic. Perhaps others as well, but I cannot recall individual instances now. Right now, what comes to mind is Dr. Vukic, from Banja Luka. He used to use that term "Turk" very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a term -- we have heard some evidence in this case in the course of which it got shouted out from a crowd at a public meeting. Is that a situation in which you are familiar with having heard the use of the word or heard of the use of the word "Turks" in a derogatory sense?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seldom attended large gatherings in Bosnia. Therefore, I do not know about that. I attended two or three gatherings in Bosnia in 1990. One was in Crni Lug, in Grahovo, and in Drvar. Those were public gatherings, and I do not remember such terms used there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you aware of any public statements in which Mr. Krajisnik has used such a term?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you remember no private occasion on which Mr. Krajisnik has used such a term; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember any particular occasion, specific occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to press you, but on that, Mr. Babic, just explain what I mean here. You might not remember any specific occasion on which you have had porridge for breakfast, but be sure that you have had sometimes porridge for breakfast. So I'm going to press you to answer my question, put it in this form: Do you say that you have ever heard Mr. Krajisnik use that term?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall Mr. Krajisnik using that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your statement at -- it's paragraph 9, and again, I don't think I need trouble you to have the statement in front of you. It's a very short, fairly simple point. You said that: "Krajisnik, Mr. Krajisnik, was a strong proponent of replacing the western variant of Serbian speech with the Eastern. When he came to Knin in 1993, when I was mayor, he inquired why we hadn't made the transition. The apparent purpose was to have the Serbs separate in all ways, including their speech. Along with others in Knin, I considered this foolish and unnecessary." Now, my case manager, who knows everything, has told me more than I ever thought I would hear or know about the language issues, but I -- the position is this: That there's something called Ekavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is called Ekavian dialect in the Serbo-Croatian language. So Ekavica is a more vulgar term than Ekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I apologise for that. Is this what we're talking about, then? You've given it the correct label, apparently. That's what we're talking about, are we, that Mr. Krajisnik was a proponent of? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's what you speak, Mr. Babic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Currently, I'm mixing dialects, because I was born in an area where Ikavian dialect was used, then I was schooled in Ekavian. So it's a mixture. When I speak to my mother, I most frequently used Ikavian dialect because that's what she is accustomed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, very interesting topic. I'm sure the Trial Chamber don't want to know today a huge amount about the details, so I won't go any further there. But I would like to ask you, then: What is -- what's the point that you were making? Because there must be one in paragraph 9 of your statement? In other words, so what if Mr. Krajisnik is keen on this particular language issue.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, this is one aspect of the issue advocated by Mr. Krajisnik. So it's one aspect, one dimension of it, which, in my view, has a role to separate, to draw a line of division, more psychologically in a way. Basically, the aim is to make a distinction between people using two different variants. Mr. Krajisnik wanted to unify the Serbian language among the Serbian people, on one hand, so that there shouldn't be any problems in communication. Because this is the same language, even though there are two dialects. So in a linguistic sense, there was this movement to unify the language, and this issue has existed both in Serbian and in Croatian for decades. In my view, Mr. Krajisnik advocated the unification of the Serbian linguistic standards, and he wanted the Ekavian variant to become dominant one. This is one side of it. And another side that existed in Bosnia, that was also advocated by Mr. Krajisnik was to separate this group from other groups, such as, for example, Croats, who also used Ekavian dialect, just like Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this dimension of introducing Ekavian dialect Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in Bosnia and Herzegovina among the Serbs there had also this aspect aimed at separating this group from other linguistic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this is -- this other dimension, this other aspect that is contained in my written statement. In my view, this other component, this other aspect, is not a communicational one, but rather psychological and emotional one. This is how I see this attempt to separate people, more on the psychological dimension than on any others. I believe this to be ridiculous and unnatural, because Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina traditionally have always spoken Ikavian dialect, and I know this because a lot of people saw this attempt as an unnatural imposition of something that doesn't come natural to them. This is why we refused this in Knin, because we found this to be unnatural attempt to change linguistic standards which were deeply rooted in Krajina and in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you've made it clear in your statement, and that's reinforced by what you've just said, Mr. Babic, that you considered, the phrase used in your statement, Mr. Krajisnik's position and attitude to this to be foolish and unnecessary, and that's clear from what you've just said. But do you say -- is it any more than that? Is that what you're saying? Does it go beyond being foolish and unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were two dimensions. One was to unify linguistic standards among all Serbs, which goes along with a political position of Mr. Krajisnik on unitarisation [phoen] and unification of all Serbs. So this is just one element of that unitarisation of Serbs. The other one, the other dimension, is, in my view, inappropriate and detrimental to international relations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is this attempt to separate and to distinguish one group from other groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a separatist tendency, which is not only ridiculous and foolish but has also much stronger political connotations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I should make it clear, because there's a very difficult one that when what gets translated into English is as "international" there and I understand the interpreters' difficulties means "between nations", that talking about it in between nations within the country concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In -- when listening, it was inter, and then a small pause, and then national.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right. For transcript readers in due course, I wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, Mr. Babic, and the reference here is at page 36 and 37 of the transcript, you - at least I think it is - you referred to meeting Mr. Seselj. Whether that's the precise page reference, I'm not absolutely sure, but it probably doesn't matter, because you clearly did refer to that anyway. The -- Mr. -- is it fair to say that Mr. Seselj was - I hope I'm reasonably near the pronunciation - could be described as a hard-liner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you implying that I used that term or is this a new question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. My question to you, Mr. Babic. You didn't use any such terms that got translated as hard-liner. You would understand what I mean, however it's coming across to you in translation, but you would understand what I mean by hard-liner, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say what you understand under that term, the hard-liner. Perhaps you should explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I should, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Babic. I think I should, then. Somebody taking the position he took, which in Mr. Seselj's case was that he was a strong nationalist, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even more than that, or shall I say even worse than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps the best thing, Mr. Babic, is to ask you to describe what you saw as Mr. Seselj's political position.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply speaking, his political platform was the creation of the Greater Serbia in the territories, regardless of whether the Serbs represented majority in those territories or not. This went against basic principles of democratic self-determination of peoples, and this represented an imposition of a national will of hegemony of one ethnic groups, in this case, the Serbs. To me this is more than extreme nationalism. I'm not a political scientist, so I couldn't really give you a proper qualification of this. But this is how I see it. Now, as to the specific attitude that he had with respect to my political views, he was against my political views, which were for self-determination of nations, starting from the municipality as a basic administrative unit in the former Yugoslavia, which was seen as the smallest unit where this self-determination could have been implemented. The municipality was defined in the constitution of federal Yugoslavia and of other republics as the smallest administrative unit, at least that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Mr. Tieger, actually, the reference was correct, 36 and 37, you were asked by Mr. Tieger yesterday about Mr. Seselj, and did he identify the borders of Greater Serbia, the state in which all Serbs should reside, to which your answer was: Yes. You were not then asked what he did identify as the borders of Greater Serbia. So that supplementary question, then, is the one I'm putting to you now. What did Mr. Seselj identify as the borders of Greater Serbia, the state in which all Serbs should reside?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said very precisely that the western borders of the Greater Serbia would go from Karlobag, Ogulin, Karlovac, Virovitica, and then the eastern and other borders would be former borders of the existing Yugoslavia. So his project would include a lot of territory, perhaps two thirds or three quarters of Croatia. The entire Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Macedonia. This was his project of Greater Serbia. He advocated it, printed maps, printed various publications, elaborated on this. So this was well known. The concept of the Greater Serbia that he advocated was well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you talked about his project. How did you understand Mr. Seselj had in mind that this goal would be achieved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By using force. By occupying the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what is the -- as far as you can remember, what is the earliest time at which you remember this being Mr. Seselj's position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that starting on the 25th of July, 1990, when he came to Srb, in my view, he wanted to compromise the Serbian Assembly which was meeting in Srb at the time. He had with him one of the first editions of a magazine called "The Greater Serbia". I did not meet him personally, but other people said that some hundred thousand people went to the local stadium where the rally was held, the local assembly, and Seselj went in another column, carrying the magazine called "The Greater Serbia". So he passed through this mass of people and everybody saw him. I remember that Croatian media reported not only on the Srb rally, Srb assembly, but also on Seselj. They reported in great detail.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. This magazine called The Greater Serbia, as far as I remember this is the first time this has been mentioned in the course of this trial, where was it published?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was published by Seselj. Whether it was under the auspices of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and later on by the Serbian Radical Party, I don't know. I don't know where it was published either. But it was published by him. I know that it is currently being published by the Serbian Radical Party. That party is the publisher of that magazine currently, and Seselj is the chairman of that party. Therefore, he and his party or his movement are the publishers. I don't know where it is being printed, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think we'll worry about the details of where it's actually physically printed, Mr. Babic. The -- Mr. Seselj is the president of that party now. That's what you've just said. When did he first become the president of that party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj initially established the Serbian Chetnik Movement, which exists to this day, and he, Mr. Seselj, has the rank of the Chetnik Vojvoda, which was conferred to him by Momcilo Djuic. I don't know whether he transformed this movement or established in parallel the Serbian Radical Party. I don't know that. I couldn't tell you exactly when this party was first set up, but I know that in Krajina it emerged in early 1992. This is when it started creating local boards. And I'm sure that it existed in 1991 as well. So the party might have been established in 1990 or in 1991, but I couldn't tell you exactly when. Following the falling apart of a group where he, Mirko Jovic, and Draskovic were together, I think that movement was called the Serbian Renewal Movement or something like that. So they split. Draskovic organised his party, Jovic organised his party, and Seselj organised the Serbian Chetnik Movement, which later on transformed itself into the Serbian Radical Party, or perhaps they existed in parallel; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just very briefly, because if we need to know more, we can go along if necessary further. But Momcilo Djuic that you mentioned, who was he? Is he, or was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about him from history, from what people said about him. He was, before World War II, an orthodox priest in the village of Strmica near Knin. During World War II, or at the beginning of World War II, he renounced his priesthood and participated in the uprising of Serbs against the Independent State of Croatia and the fascist occupation of Yugoslavia, in the ranks of the Serbian Ravna Gora Movement. That was a Chetnik movement led by General Draza Mihajlovic. He was a commander in the Second World War of the so-called military formation which was called the Dinara Chetnik division. In 1944, in October, or in December, he left Knin with a large number of his unit members. He withdrew to Italy, where the allied forces transferred him and his followers to Western countries. They mostly went to Great Britain, Canada, and the United States. He went to the United States, to California, where he founded an organisation, an association of citizens. I don't know exactly what it was called under US laws. But it was a Serbian Chetnik Movement, a non-profit organisation, and he was the organisation's president. And he was at its head up until a couple of years ago, when he died. He continued to hold the rank of a Chetnik Vojvoda, which was conferred on him in World War II. I don't know the rules of the organisation, but under those rules, he had the right to confer the title to other -- on other people. So he could name or appoint new Vojvodas. So that is what he did for Dr. Vojislav Seselj. He conferred on him the title of Chetnik Vojvoda during his visit to the United States. I don't know whether this was in 1989 or 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Returning to Dr. Seselj: Is he -- what, he's a man in his 60s now, is he, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj is a few years older than I am. I don't think he's in the 60s. He's two or three years older than I am, so he's maybe around 50. I think that he was born in 1952 or 1954. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. That's quite specific enough for my purposes. Thank you. When you first became aware of the Radical Party and Dr. Seselj, what was your own degree of political activity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, a president of the party's municipal board, president of the Knin municipality, and president of the Serbian national council. I think at the time I was already the president of the Serbian National Council. In 1990, at the end of summer or the beginning of the fall, in Belgrade, I met him in Belgrade. So I did know about him or of him as of July 25th. Before that, I heard about Vojislav Seselj and his party. I heard that he had fled from Sarajevo because he was politically persecuted and arrested by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And after he served a long sentence in the prison in Zenica, he moved to Belgrade. I know for sure that for a while he was at the same employment bureau as I was. I know that he was there on the records like I was, of the same bureau. I was on the same bureau as a high school graduate, because at that time I hadn't completed my university degree. So the same officer who held my files and he said that he was looking for a job for him as well because he had just moved to Belgrade and that he was a lawyer. As far as his party, it appeared in Krajina at the end of 1990. It existed in 1991. I'm not sure exactly when the party was founded, whether this was in 1990 or 1991. I think I've already talked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you say that back in -- well, let's say 1991, because the period you've just given includes of course the later year. Would you say in 1991 that Dr. Seselj's party was less influential in the politics of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your part of Croatia than your own party, the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said something wrong -- something to the effect that it had a lesser influence than my own party. I don't know. Perhaps the question wasn't interpreted properly. Could the interpreter please repeat the whole question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that the easier way of doing it? I can repeat the question, if that's the more suitable way of doing it. I think it probably is. The --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some confusion in the question. The interpreter missed something and then added something. I would like to hear the whole question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can clear up the question over a break, if this is the time that the Trial Chamber would wish to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is approximately the time we usually have our break, so if it would be a suitable moment for you, then we would adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness may be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Stewart, as far as your letter is concerned, although we gave it some attention, I can't give you any results of the -- of our considerations at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I think we finished somewhere where a question was about to be repeated for Mr. Babic. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think there was, unusually, there was one slight slip in the way the question was transmitted to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I was asking you, Mr. Babic, was whether, in 1991, Mr. Seselj's party was significantly less influential in the politics of your part of Croatia than your own party.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I think -- or rather, I'm sure that in 1991, the Serbian Radical Party did not exist in the ARK Krajina in an organised manner. I don't know whether it existed in Eastern Slavonia. I'm not sure. As far as the influence of the parties, that's something that I would like to say. Something that was characteristic for the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the Radical Party of Vojislav Seselj. The movement and the party, it's a leader party, so the leader is the person who promotes and represents the party. So it would be more correct here to speak about the influence of Dr. Vojislav Seselj on political events rather than the influence of his party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Babic, that slightly seems to follow from what you've said. In 1991, then, do we understand you to be saying that, in line with the answer you've just given, the Serbian Radical Party didn't exist in an organised manner, but Dr. Seselj existed and was active and a person to be certainly noted in the politics of your part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you regard him as a positive, negative, or neutral influence and force in those politics?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that his first appearances were counter-productive. They were very negative. The influence over the political processes that were under way in Croatia in 1990 was negative. It was a radical discrediting of the politics or the policies conducted by Serbian leaders in Croatia at the time. So in that sense, we can say that this is something that also happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you described -- I just want to explore with you a bit the -- Mr. -- Dr. Seselj's platform, as I think it has been called. You said that he had in mind that his goal, his Greater Serbia goal, would be achieved by violence. Can you -- did you know any more in 1991, let's say? Let's take the middle of 1991 as our point of reference for the moment. Did you know more about the means by which such a goal was to be achieved through violence, according to Dr. Seselj's platform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you speaking formally about the platform? If that -- if this is the topic that we're speaking about, specifically the platform, are we speaking about the platform in general or are we speaking about the platform specifically? But I can respond precisely to the latter part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've asked me a question by way of clarification, Mr. Babic. I'm not -- I used the word "platform," which is what comes across in translation. I'm not confining my question to any formal document or pronouncement. To clarify, then, I am asking you whether you knew more in mid-1991 about the means by which Dr. Seselj's goal of the Greater Serbia was, as far as his views are concerned, to be achieved through violence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say what I know. In mid-1991, and if we're talking about May, on that day I found out from Vojislav Seselj that his volunteers were taking part in the fighting in Borovo Selo against the Croatia police and that two of them were killed. So I don't know. At that time through his volunteers he was taking part in the fighting which the so-called parallel structure, the Serbian DB and the Serbs from Borovo Selo were waging against the Croatian government. I know about that specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you is this, Mr. Babic: You gave your evidence earlier this week, yesterday and in your statement, you have given your evidence about Dr. Seselj. You have referred to Dr. Seselj's Greater Serbia policy, if I just give it that brief label. You have told the Trial Chamber this morning that the means by which Dr. Seselj was apparently going to achieve that goal was by violence. So that's what you've said you know so far. So now I'm asking you what else, if anything, you know about the methods and strategy, if you like, which Dr. Seselj had expressed, which were apparent to you, for the achievement of his goal.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention the word "apparently" in any sense. As far as a response to your question, I told you already one piece of information. This is another piece of information from November 1991. Vojislav Seselj at the time was a professor in Pristina, and through the media he was explaining the objectives that it was necessary to occupy Slunj in Croatia and Vukovar as soon as possible and that these were military priorities in the operations. In that period, I can't remember specifically the time he explained that it was necessary for the army to take up the borders, the Karlobag-Ogulin-Virovitica line. This was at the end of December in 1991, and in early 1992, when he armed his volunteers himself, and he armed them for the conflicts that were taking place against the army of Croatia. He supported them. This was something that was organised by the Serbian Ministry of Defence. These are some specific details that I recall at this time from that period. I also know that when the war in Bosnia started, this was publicly broadcast over television that he was confirming the title of Chetnik Vojvoda to the commanders of his units, the ones that were fighting in Bosnia in the Romanija area and the Pale area. This is what I recall; I do not wish to improvise on anything. This is as much as I want to say. I also remember that at a rally on the 2nd of May, near Plitvice, I listened to his conversation with General Andrija Raseta. General Raseta was the deputy commander of the Zagreb army district at the time and he was holding the buffer zone around the Plitvice hotels in relation to the Croatian police. At this rally, he met with Andrija Raseta, Seselj, and I listened to a conversation which was at the time interesting to me. I wasn't quite knowledgeable about the hierarchy of the Serbian Chetnik Movement at the time. So I heard from Seselj in person when he was explaining to Raseta that the Vojvoda rank was -- corresponded to the rank of colonel in the JNA. At the time, on May 2nd, 1992 -- 1991, he introduced himself as a Chetnik Vojvoda, an equivalent rank to the rank of colonel in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to be fair to you. In the course of that answer, you said you "didn't wish to improvise on anything. This is as much as I want to say." Do I understand when you say "this is as much as I want to say" that in fact you were saying this is as much as you can say on the subject?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as my specific knowledge is concerned, I do not want to generalise. I want to tell you some specific details. Of course, I mentioned his public advocacy that the army should take up the borders of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line, and I also told you about some things that I heard about him and that some -- and also some things which I heard directly from him. I wanted to be specific. I did not wish to improvise. I wanted to be specific about what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the Radical Party, whenever exactly it was formed, that -- I think you described as being a leader party, so that it made more sense to talk in terms of what Dr. Seselj said and thought and did than the party. But was it -- well, it wasn't a one-man party, presumably. Did Mr. -- Dr. Seselj have any identifiable associates who were also influential in support of his policies and his party, in whatever formal or informal way it existed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said a leadership or a leader party, I was thinking of the way the party was organised, where the leader enjoys a considerable amount of authority. When I was talking about a leader party and the way it presented itself in the media, the way it presented its policy, what I meant was that Dr. Vojislav Seselj held the main word. He was the promotor of the party. Of course, its hierarchy and organisation was also operative. But at the time, it had this organisational structure in Serbia, and Dr. Vojislav Seselj, assisted by the socialist party and its voters, was elected as a deputy to the Serbian parliament at the time, as a representative of that party. However, when we're talking about the territory of Croatia and the Krajina area, as well as Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 1990 and 1991, we viewed Dr. Seselj as the president of the Serbian Radical Party, a person who had a lot of media influence personally, not only as a party person, but personally, a person who was a Chetnik Vojvoda, who had his military formations and volunteers in Croatia and in Bosnia. So in that sense, in the 1991 period, that is how I am referring to Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask you, I got the impression that this was not an answer to your question. Since you asked any identifiable associates who were also influential. So I thought that you were asking for persons on the top level in that party, close associates to Mr. Seselj. I would not mind if you would then interfere and ask the witness to answer your question. Mr. Babic, I'm not saying that it's not interesting what you tell us, but it was not an answer to the question of Mr. Stewart. Would you please listen carefully to his questions and answer specifically what he asks you. If he wants to be more, you can be assured that he'll ask you for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, Mr. Babic can be assured. I'm grateful for that, Your Honour. I'd be particularly careful this morning. I haven't wanted to interrupt Mr. Babic. So I am grateful for Your Honour's help in relation to such a matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yes, in principle, you could take it that I would like answers as specifically as you can manage to my questions. So I was asking you if you could give some names of other people at the top of Dr. Seselj's organisation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that as far as the people who were in the organisation of Dr. Vojislav Seselj and his party and who were relevant for Krajina and Croatia, I know Rade Leskovac, Rade Leskovac who was the president of the Executive Board of the Radical Party for Krajina after it was established in 1992 or 1993. I don't know exactly when. As far as the leadership of the Radical Party, I know that the deputy president of that party for several terms of office, I think from the very beginning, but I cannot be quite sure, was Tomislav Nikolic. Todorovic was the president of the Executive Board. I'm trying to remember the other names. I know some other people, of course, but at the moment I cannot recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If they come back into your mind, Mr. Babic, please let the Trial Chamber know at any point. The -- my case on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik is that he never met Dr. Seselj. Do you know anything that would contradict that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. Krajisnik had a meeting with Mr. Seselj in autumn of 1992 in Bosanski Novi. That was a gathering or an assembly presided over by Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Seselj was a speaker there. I don't know whether they sat together during the break. However, Seselj did address the gathering. I cannot remember the exact moment when he went to the podium to speak; however, I remember him sitting in the first Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. row. I remember that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should qualify something I said. It's -- I don't say that Mr. Krajisnik has never in his whole life met Dr. Seselj, but my case is that in 1991 and 1992, or before that, he hadn't. But you've given your answer on that. In relation to 1992, anyway, so there clearly is a difference identified. Can you then give more specific details about that meeting with -- in Bosanski Novi? You say the autumn of 1992. Are you able to be more specific about the date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was between August and the assembly that was held in Prijedor at the end of October. So sometime during that period. I cannot give you the exact date. I received information that the assembly of Republika Srpska and the assembly of Republika Srpska Krajina was held there, as I was a deputy of the assembly of Republika Srpska Krajina, I went to see what was going on, although I did not have an official invitation. I came there convinced that it was a joint assembly, but when I saw what was going there, I wasn't so sure about that. The people were gathered there, some 120 people, in a hotel in Bosanski Novi. Mr. Krajisnik and some other people presided over the event. I think that there were some people from Krajina there as well. I was late in arriving, and I went before the assembly ended. I saw that Dr. Seselj was present. He gave a speech very typical of him, about Serbian unification and unification of Serbian lands. I couldn't give you any more specifics, but this is what I remember about that gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you say it was after the funeral of Mr. Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I'm not sure exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You think it was after the funeral; is that your position? But you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So where your statement, in paragraph 8, expressed that in unqualified terms, which is does in the third sentence, "this meeting in Bosanski Novi was after the funeral for Raskovic," you're now telling the Trial Chamber, it's apparent from your answer, that you can't express it in those unqualified terms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, because I cannot remember the exact date. In my view, I could say with great reliability that that was between funeral of Raskovic and the assembly in Prijedor, which was in late October. The funeral was in late August. The assembly was held in late October in Prijedor. So most likely it was in that period of time, but, as I cannot recall the date, I cannot guarantee this. This was why I say "most likely."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Babic, it's not just that you can't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to make it clear, Mr. Babic. It isn't just now that you can't recall the date; it's that you have reduced your degree of assurance about it being before or after the funeral of Mr. Raskovic, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain that that was between the funeral of Mr. Raskovic and the other event. And I say this with a very great degree of certainty that that was between the funeral and the other event, although there is a minor possibility that it was held at another time. But definitely before the end of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you were, as you clearly were, politically active in 1991 and 1992, did you keep a diary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a diary, but some kind of a notebook where I would record what happened during the meetings and so on. I did that quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you didn't keep a diary of your future and forthcoming appointments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally not. I simply noted down what happened at the meetings or during the events where I was present. Sometimes I would do it during the event itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you working as -- well, you were a working politician, no doubt, but were you working in some other paid activity during 1991 and 1992, alongside your political activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My paid function was president of municipality of Knin from May of 1992 until early 1994. This was my paid function. This was my job for which I was paid. And then from 1994 and on to 1995, I don't think that's relevant, because your question pertained to 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Babic. You said you didn't keep a diary. Was a diary kept for you by a secretary or personal assistant in your office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, I had my notes about the events. I did not have a typical diary that I would keep every day. I simply occasionally wrote down some notes. My secretary would also record various things, telephone calls, meetings, and so on. Yes, she had her own notes too, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you a question, Mr. Stewart, not being a native speaker. Mr. Stewart, you're asking about a diary and at the same time you refer to a future and forthcoming appointments, which I would put as -- I would call that an agenda. Is there any confusion about a book in which you write down appointments and a book in which you write down whatever you experienced or what you intend to do or what you have experienced? I'm not quite sure. I also understand from the witness's answers that he seems to say "I did write down what I experienced," which I would do in a different book from where my appointments are written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We all have different practices, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I, after a hundred or a couple of hundred years, giving up the battle to try to get the English version of the English language adopted throughout the United States. The difference between agenda and diary, Your Honour, is basically a difference between English and American, with respect. What we would call a diary in England is commonly called an agenda by Americans, which is simply I'm afraid why I use the word "diary." I therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but just to avoid the confusion, when the witness answers to the existence of any notes written down where you were seeking other information, that might be -- if there's no confusion, fine, but it came into my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had -- I take Your Honour's point. I had attempted to deal with that confusion by very expressly, it's just gone offer the top of the screen, by very expressly referring to a diary of forthcoming appointments. I had really tried very hard to make that distinction to avoid the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, the answers of the witness mainly relate to what he experienced during meetings and not -- Mr. Babic, has it become clear to you that Mr. Stewart was asking you whether there was any book in which you would write down any appointments for the future, apart from perhaps writing down notes on what was said or what you thought or -- well, whatever? Was that clear to you? And if not, would you then please respond to the question whether you kept in a book a record of meetings you would have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I said. The question was whether I kept a diary. In our language, a diary is something where you record your daily events, things that happened that day. I said that I did not keep that kind of a book. I would occasionally write down notes after the events, or sometimes even during the meeting I would note down what was transpiring at the meeting. I did not make notes and plans for forthcoming meetings, except that occasionally in my calendar I would write down that on such-and-such date I was supposed to have a meeting. I would do that occasionally, but not regularly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the word "calendar" is introduced. That's how it is on my computer as well. If you want to write down an appointment, it goes under the part where it says calendar. I don't know whether you referred to that, but I will not further interfere. It seemed there was some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there may be. The calendar is an American phrase for this reason. We use it in a different way. So I am, I hope, if somebody looks at the transcripts and thinks this is an incompetent way of dealing with it, I won't lose any sleep over that. The -- I specifically attempted to make it absolutely clear what I was talking about and I believed I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I am asking you whether -- and if you've already answered it, then I'm afraid that's too bad because we're just going to have to get it clear. I am asking you whether you kept any sort of book, notebook, in which were noted future appointments, so that next Wednesday, the 25th of whatever it is, you're going to such-and-such a meeting. So that it reminds you that you've got to go, so you don't lose track of it and miss things. Did you have any sort of book, notebook, notes of that form in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I would occasionally write that down or I would circle a date in the calendar as a day when I had something to attend. I would note down that, yes, something was forthcoming on such-and-such date, and what exactly it was. I would do it occasionally, not regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Babic, do you agree it's very clear from what you've just said that if you could circle a date in the calendar as a day when you had something to attend, then that notebook in which you were doing that circling was exactly the sort of thing I'm describing, whether it's called a diary, calendar, agenda, whether that comes across as three different words in your language, that's what you had, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had those kinds of papers. So it wasn't one document or book, but different ones. Sometimes that would be a small calendar that I would carry in my pocket. Sometimes it would be a notebook in which I would record events. Sometimes I would simply write it down on a piece of paper that was in my pocket. So I had those kinds of notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, does any -- do any of those items, does any of that material that you've described of yours survive today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So which do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have something dating from 1994 and 1995, whereas for 1990 and 1991, that remained back in my apartment in Knin. So there is some documentation there. After the Croatian operation called Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever been asked, in connection with any interview given to -- in relation to this Tribunal, have you ever been asked for any such material?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me generally whether I had a diary, and I responded that I would occasionally keep notes. But they didn't ask me to surrender any notes, no. They asked me for documentation pertaining to certain events. I did have some documentation, and I was able to trace it. I had documentation for a specific reason, which I explained during the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we be clear, then, Mr. Babic, of this material that you have referred to over the last two or three minutes, has any of it at any time been handed over by you, obviously temporally, has any of it ever been handed over by you, obviously temporally, has any of it ever been handed over by you to any investigator or interviewer in connection with any proceedings or prospective or possible proceedings in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that kind of material, except for official documents. So I had a large number of official documents and I turned that over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who has access to your apartment in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that a Croatian colonel lives there now. Now, who had access to my apartment prior to him, I don't know. I assume Croatian authorities sent some other people there, because they are the ones which let other persons have the use of my apartment. I assume that Croatian authorities did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, if anybody else knows, I don't. You'll simply have to, please, say. Were you arrested or did you surrender voluntarily in relation to the indictment against you before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I surrendered voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 26th of November of last year. Last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at that time, when you surrendered voluntarily, was the material that you've -- these documents that you've just referred to over the last five minutes or so, it is now in your apartment in Knin as you describe?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you mean the notes or the documents of other kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Any of it, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly was in my apartment in Knin at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, it was your evidence about this material. You are the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one who told the Trial Chamber where it was. I don't know, Mr. Babic. I'm just asking the questions. The material which you have referred to over the last six minutes or so, where was it -- well, was it in your apartment in Knin when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material that I turned over to the investigators of the Tribunal in 1991 was with me in Belgrade at the time, and this was what I turned over to the investigators. The remaining documentation, the one which remained in my apartment in 1995, I don't know where it is now, nor do I know who had access to it. In November of last year, I didn't know where the material from my apartment was. I don't know exactly to which material you are referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before further confusion arises, I'd like to put one or two questions to Mr. Babic. Mr. Babic, when were you for the last time in your apartment in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 2nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I'm going to have to scroll back to what the witness said a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question came into my mind when the witness referred to the Operation Storm. So therefore, I got the impression that you asked questions on the basis that Mr. Babic would have lived in his apartment until late last year and then voluntarily surrendered. I'm not sure that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wasn't making -- I don't make too many assumptions, Your Honour, when I just don't know something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did put this question to the witness, and you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, I do need to scroll back to see what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What you said, Mr. Babic, was, and this is at -- it's at 21 -- 38:21. 38:21 is the reference. Thank you. It's at 11:35:16. I'd asked you just above that: "Mr. Babic, does any, do any of those items, does any of that material that you've described of yours survive today?" You said: "Very few." So I asked, not surprisingly: "So which do?" That being the clear implication of what you were saying. Your answer was: "I have something dating from 1994 and 1995, whereas for 1990 and 1991, that remained back in my apartment in Knin, so there is some documentation there after the Croatian operation called Storm." So my questions since then have proceeded, not surprisingly, Mr. Babic, on the basis of your answers, because you're the one that knows. That is why I'm asking you those things. But let's be clear, please, Mr. Babic. You've told the Tribunal there is some documentation there. Not -- now, of course I know you haven't been anywhere --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. Perhaps it was a slip of tongue on my part or not. How would I know whether there is any documentation in my apartment remaining from 1995? All I said was that the documentation stayed, remained, in my apartment in 1995, and I don't know who had access to it, who has had access in the meantime. So I don't know what remained of it. There is a Croatian colonel living there, and I don't know what happened to my items which were left there after the 4th or 5th of August of 1995. I referred to the documentation that I had with me when I said that in 2001 I turned that over to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. Babic, there was another slip of the tongue in your answer there, because when you said: "How would I know whether there was any documentation in my apartment remaining from 1995," in fact I was asking you specifically about the documentation which you had referred to from the period -- now, I don't remember whether you said 1990, 1991, or 1991 and 1992, but that's not a material difference. So that was -- do you agree, that was a slip of the tongue? We were talking about the earlier period, weren't we?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I said whether it remained, I know that it remained, that it was left behind, but whether it is still there, whether somebody came into the apartment, threw it away, burnt it, whether Croatian police seized the documentation, that's what I don't know. I don't know what happened to it after I left. I know that it was left behind when I left. My books, my clothes, my items, my property. I know that it was left behind. But whether after the Storm operation somebody came in, seized it, burned it, threw it away, I don't know what happened to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I do understand what you were saying there now. This sometimes does happen as we pass through the languages and so on. I do see what you're saying there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask you. I would be interested to know whether the witness testified about any notes, documents, whatever, in 1994, 1995. And then he moved to 1990 and 1991. What happened with anything that was created in 1992 or 1993 still remains unclear. I don't know whether it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I quite agree. It's a -- we -- we're trying to do these other things, but I quite agree, it's a gap to be plugged if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We -- as His Honour correctly points out, Mr. Babic, we've talked about documentation from 1990 and 1991, and perhaps 1992. We talked about documentation from 1994 and 1995. What about the period in between? What about such items in relation to the period 1993 and I think possibly early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've been explaining, I spoke about two different periods. I was an official of Krajina up until February of 1992, and this is one period of my political activity. Following that, I was in a way ostracised. I was in opposition. I was president of the Knin municipality. However, that's a different period in my political life. And starting in April of 1994, I became a minister in the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, may I stop you? Would you again listen carefully to the question. The question is whether any of such documents, any -- I would say any written remainders of where you would have written down when and with whom to meet, at what days, whether they do still exist. If it's a different period, fine, and if you were in a different position, but that's not the question. The question is whether there were any remainders of this kind of documents in the period 1993 -- 1992 and 1993. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one, I believe, small matter of clarification, Your Honour. That's the reference in the last line of the witness's answer to becoming a minister in the Bosnian government in April of 1994. I believe that that may require some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly if it's literally true, Your Honour, it would cast a different light on all sorts of things, so it probably does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Might be the third slip of the tongue or a wrong translation, but we do not know yet. But please proceed. But, Mr. Babic, before entering into this new issue which Mr. Stewart certainly will seek clarification, could you answer his last question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a minister of foreign affairs in the government of Republika Srpska Krajina. Just to correct the record. And as for the other, I think I was clear. I said that my private notes that I had for 1991 and 1992 and 1990 were in my apartment in Knin, and they were left behind after I left in August of 1995. Some official documents, some documents from the archives that I had about the events from 1991 and 1992 in Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I have to stop you again. The question was not, and you are now repeating your answers on the earlier documents, the question was about 1992 and 1993. So that's the period not covered yet by your answers. Please answer the question of Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have some notes from 1993, 1994, and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you just briefly indicate the circumstances in which you did leave your apartment in Knin in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called by the American ambassador from Zagreb, Peter Galbraith, to continue talk about the Z 4 plan and the proposal of the international community for the Krajina, and to discuss topics such as the implementation of the economic agreement with Croatia and the question of the engagement of the Serbian army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina in the Bihac pocket.
