So at the invitation of Mr. Galbraith I went to the American embassy in Belgrade to talk with him. There were two proposals where these talks should take place, Brod, at Jadran or the US embassy in Belgrade. So we agreed to meet at the US embassy in Belgrade where we had this meeting. After that I did not manage to return to Knin. Because in the meantime, the Croatian offensive or the Croatian operation Storm began.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you living with your family in the apartment in Knin up to the time -- up to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my wife, two children, and my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you went to Belgrade to have these talks with the US embassy and others perhaps, did your wife -- just shorthand: Did your wife remain for the time being in the apartment in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She took her mother to a regular -- for regular treatment at the oncology clinic in Belgrade. Her mother was ill, so she had to go for regular treatments at the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- what is the -- I'll rephrase the question, then. Did any of your wife and children remain living in the apartment in Knin when you went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the last one to leave the apartment, and I locked the apartment after I left. My wife was at the hospital with her mother, and my children were on their summer vacation with my sister. So when I left the apartment at that time, I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Expecting to return?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you know -- do you know anything about what happened to your apartment -- well, first question is, then, you talk about Operation Storm. You've referred to those difficulties. When did that begin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which was how long after you had left to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I left perhaps on the 2nd or the 1st of August. It was one day after my statement and the agreement with Ambassador Galbraith that we accept all agreements in order to resolve the situation in Krajina. So these were the circumstances. I don't know how many days had passed. This was within two or three, or three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it in fact just -- whether it's good, bad, or whatever. Was it in fact just luck or chance that this offensive began just a few days after all of you had left the flat in Knin, or did you -- I'll add to that question. Or did you anticipate such trouble and, therefore, move you and yourself, family, out for that reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a coincidence. As far as I'm personally concerned, I can say that the political circumstances and the reasons why the Croatian offensive began at that time, I can say that I was the president of the Krajina for seven days at the time. I accepted the negotiations of the international community to resolve the Krajina status. Our delegation in Geneva also agreed to those negotiations. After that, there was a response by the Croat representative that Serbs were allegedly buying sometime for something, and that was their pretext for them not to enter into the negotiations and to accept the agreement and for suddenly implementing the operation in Krajina. My interpretation was that Croatia, because of our agreement to negotiations, carried out that operation immediately in order to prevent those negotiations from taking place. This is my interpretation of why Croatia carried out that aggression or that operation to occupy the Krajina and to expel the population, the Serb population from Krajina at that time. But this is not something that was a topic of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the position is this, is it, that at that time, in early August 1995, your expectation was that, subject to dealing with your mother's medical condition and problems, your wife was expected to return to Knin, that at the end of their summer holidays away with, I think it was your sister, your children were expected to return to the apartment in Knin, and subject to your political obligations and meetings and commitments, you were also expecting to return to the apartment in Knin? Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that you mentioned my sister. My sister did not live in Knin. She lived in Belgrade. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. We can read the transcript on that one, Mr. Babic. And is it -- you may have already said this. Is it correct, you have never even once gone back to your apartment in Knin since then? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And as far as you know, has -- have any of your wife, any other member of your family, ever gone back to the apartment in Knin since then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Has anybody else ever gone back to the apartment in Knin at your request or on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except on that day when the people from Knin were leaving. I'm not sure whether the neighbour who had the key to our apartment went into the apartment or not. But nobody entered the apartment at the request of myself or my family. After a while, we asked some of our neighbours who had left who was living in our apartment, and we got the reply that a Croat army colonel was living in the apartment and that it was not possible to have access to the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the position has been for a very -- obviously it is now, Mr. Babic. I don't wish to be flippant, but the position has been for a number of years that you have not been able safely to go back to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly since when, but since the Croatian prosecution in Split or Sibenik issued an indictment against me for secession from Croatia, for separating off from Croatia. There were court proceedings conducted of a political nature on charges of secession from Croatia and for jeopardising the territorial integrity of Croatia. These court proceedings ended in a verdict which, under the law of amnesty adopted by the Croatian assembly, was annulled. But regardless of that, I never felt safe enough to go back to Croatia. I was pardoned or amnestied under the Croatian law, but I have not yet entertained the thought of going back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When was the -- I apologise. I normally like to be on top of such details, Mr. Babic, rather than having to ask you, but when was the indictment against you issued in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I found out later from the media that an indictment was issued. Exactly when it was issued, I don't know. I wasn't notified of it and I did not attend any kind of proceedings that are connected to that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When, then, did you first find out about the issue of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely. I wasn't really paying attention to that. I wasn't sure whether it was true or just a provocation. In Belgrade, after 1995, I was informed that this had actually happened, and I received some more specific information about that from people who were also on one of the indictments. So in Belgrade, after 1995, I found out more details about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you said you couldn't tell the Trial Chamber precisely when you first found out about the issue of the indictment. But can you give the Trial Chamber at least some indication of the time when you first found out about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mentioned before 1995. I think somebody reported it -- of it. But I don't know exactly when. I wasn't following the Croatian press at the time when this was discussed, so I'm really not sure. Somebody at some point told me about this before 1995, but I did not know any specifics. So I'm not able to be precise about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So before 1995 was before you'd left Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you remained in Croatia for at least some period, having had information that there was an indictment against you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Krajina, to be specific. We had the political approach that this was a part of Croatia, and it was necessary to resolve the status of that area within Croatia through political negotiations. At the time, I physically was not under the control of Croatian authorities. I lived on a separate area, where there was Serb authority, the authority of the Serbian Republic of Krajina. But we were not formally under the authority of the -- under the jurisdiction of the Croat government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is it to be understood as this, in summary, then: Although you knew about the indictment from a practical point of view, you felt safe before the time that you finally left Knin, but after that, as a result of Operation Storm, you no longer felt safe to go back to Croatia? Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, simply speaking. Yes. I believe that this was a political proceedings that was being conducted against me and that with the resolution of the political crisis, this would be resolved. However, after Storm, it was unsafe for anybody to return. All the people from Krajina were expelled, the houses were burned, crimes were taking place. It was a horrible event. Few people would have dared to go back. To this very day, a large majority of people do not dare go back, even though efforts are being made for people to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you still -- I'm making an assumption that you owned it before, but do you still own the apartment in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under laws at the time in force in Croatia and in the whole of the former Yugoslavia, I had the rights to use the apartment for an indefinite term. As for your question, if I'm still enjoying that same right under the laws of the new Croatia, I was supposed to buy back or purchase my apartment when this period -- this period to buy the apartment was at the time when the laws of the Republic of Croatia were not valid in Krajina. There is still the question that I am asking and that other people are asking. We still do not own our apartments, but we do have the right to inhabit or temporary right to -- we have the tenancy rights to this apartment and we have lost this right because we did not apply to buy the apartment within the deadlines set. This is now being set right. The Croatian government is trying to make it possible for those who had tenancy rights to buy the apartments. This is still quite an open question that is not resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you, since you left in 1995, have you made any attempt to in any way to retrieve or at least preserve any of your belongings that were in the apartment when you left in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I asked my neighbour to do, the neighbour who used to go there, is to see whether it would be possible to have access to the apartment. After I was informed that a Croatian colonel is there, was living there - his last name was Jakelic or something - I stopped, or I gave up asking for anything from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When can you say that happened, i.e., that's to say when did the Croatian colonel, as far as you know, move into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when he moved in. I think my neighbour went to the apartment a year later, perhaps in 1996 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's only that you said: "After I was --" well, I'll rephrase the question. When were you informed that a Croatian colonel was in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you say that you had an opportunity to meet with or be with Mr. Krajisnik in the period 1991 and 1992, you thought, four times. Remember? And that's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But it's also correct, isn't it, to start with that, you never had any meeting with Mr. Krajisnik at all at which only the two of you were present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I attended joint meetings with him on four occasions. Each of these four occasions were attended by Mr. Krajisnik, myself, and a large number of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Babic, that the only time that you can recall having any private discussion with Mr. Krajisnik is, so far as it was private, the discussion which you say you had with him at a dinner in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on several occasions, in 1993 for the first time, in January 1995, in May 1995, and then perhaps in late May or early June in 1995, twice. I was with him on five occasions in groups of two or three or alone. In 1993 and 1994, I think it was on five occasions that I was alone with Mr. Krajisnik or in the company of two or three other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you say that -- do you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you say that on any occasion in 1991 and 1992, that you were at the same meeting as Mr. Krajisnik, that there were as few as two or three other people present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had met him in 1993 and 1994. As far as 1991 and 1992, I said that I had attended four meetings at which Mr. Krajisnik, myself, and a lot of other people were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to, as quickly as we can, before we look at any particular meeting, I'd just like to do a sort of checklist with you, Mr. Babic, so that we know what we're talking about here. First of all, you say that you met -- I want to keep this as brief as possible. You'll get a chance to answer questions about each of these meetings, so yes or no as near as possible, please. You say you met Mr. Krajisnik on the 23rd of October, 1991, at the Federation Palace in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say that you met him on the 30th and/or the 31st of January, 1992, in Belgrade, just to remind you, at a meeting at which, among others, Mr. Mladic was present; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a three-day meeting. The 31st of January and the 1st and 2nd of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. But that meeting, anyway. We'll leave aside date discrepancies. So that's second meeting. You say that you met Mr. Krajisnik, or you were at a meeting, you were both present at a meeting in Bosanski Novi, that we've considered already this morning briefly in a slightly different context. That's the one around Mr. Raskovic's funeral. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you say that you met Mr. Krajisnik, you were both present at a meeting on the 30th and/or the 31st of October, 1992, in Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And those are, throughout 1991 and 1992, those are the four meetings that you recall at which you and Mr. Krajisnik were both present, and there are no others that you recall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. I don't recall any other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then your evidence has been, just to complete this, that after 1992, your evidence was that you met him on a number of occasions between 1993 and 1995, but you -- is it correct you are not able to be specific about how many?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember exactly. It was on five occasions, and I remember the time and the circumstances of the meetings. I don't recall if there were any others. But I know definitely the time and the circumstances for the five meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that's five meetings during the period 1993 to 1995 inclusive; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One in 1993 and four in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you never met Mr. Krajisnik at all in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct, and it would seem to tie in a bit with some of the other things you've said this morning, that after 1995, you never met Mr. Krajisnik until seeing him in this courtroom ever again? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're very close, I think, to the time where the break comes. If that isn't inconvenient to the Trial Chamber, it would be as suitable a point as any to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's take it. We'll adjourn until 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- But -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That happens when I want to become efficient and then things go completely wrong. Yes, the witness may be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would speed things up, Your Honour, of course, always, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're soliciting to have a kind of a civil law trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we ran through a sort of checklist of meetings that you say you and Mr. Krajisnik were both present at in the course of 1991 and 1992. The first one is the one you referred to in paragraph 7 of your statement, though, as far as we see, there's nothing added to it in your oral evidence given this week. You say that you believe you first met Mr. Krajisnik at a meeting on 23rd October 1991, at Federation Palace during the discussions regarding the support of Yugoslavia. First question, Mr. Babic, is: How confident are you about the date of the 23rd of October, 1991, and specifically the 23rd October? I'm not quibbling about what you're saying about the year.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confident that it was after the 20th of October, after the meeting in Banja Luka on the 18th of October, and that was before the 25th of October. Also, I believe that somewhere in my notes I had some chronology of the events, based on which I concluded that it was on the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what notes are you referring to in that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote down a chronology of events as a reminder for myself as I was preparing to meet with the investigators of the Tribunal. Based on my recollections and the documents I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you hand over that note to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My question was, Mr. Babic: Did you hand over that note to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you've already said they didn't ask you. Did you offer them to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I simply did it in order to organise my recollections for my own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you were being interviewed by the investigators, did you have that note in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the point of preparing a note to refresh your recollection and then not to have it with you at the very meeting for which it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I went to the meeting with them, I wanted to organise my thoughts, my recollections, because quite a lot of time had passed in the meantime. And at that first meeting I had with the investigator, whose name I cannot pronounce, sometime in October of 2002, I was told that, when I asked for the meeting, this investigator came as well, and they inquired as to the time and place where we could meet, and they said it would last for several days, that they were interested in the events from 1990, 1991, and 1992. They said that that was the period of time that they were interested in. And after that, I sat down and I went back in my thoughts to that time and wrote down some notes. The investigation itself lasted for quite a long time. There were four instances. And after they put questions to me, I would immerse myself back into that time, into those months, in order to organise my thoughts, and I wrote down some lists and some notes. The investigators asked me whether I had diaries, whether I had notebooks, and I gave them an answer similar to the one I gave you here today. They didn't ask me whether I was making any notes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Babic, I have to ask you again. You prepare a note to collect your thoughts about these events. You are going for a meeting with investigators for this Tribunal, which charges people with serious crimes. Having done that, you're asking this Trial Chamber to accept that you then didn't bother to take the note with you to that meeting? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the chronology of events that I wrote down for myself. I didn't know what they were going to ask me. I don't even know whether I had it with me on that occasion. I think it wasn't. I think I left it back at home, because it was made just for myself. Perhaps had somebody asked for it, I would have produced it, but at any rate, it wasn't used during the interview. Perhaps it was in my bag when I was at the meeting, but I know that I did not use it at the meeting during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by a lawyer or any other form of representative at that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An attorney was always present during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are we talking about the interviews that were held in March this year, or are we talking about an interview longer ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the interviews in October, November, December 2001, January 2001, February 2001. Oh, I apologise, I apologise. 2002. So those interviews. This is when I gave my first statement to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you referred a few minutes ago, when you were talking about this chronology that you didn't take with you or that you might have had in your bag, you said that was based on your recollection and the documents you had. So my next question, Mr. Babic, is: What were those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents I turned over to the Prosecution, the documents which were official documents from the archives pertaining to the Serbian autonomous region Krajina and Serbian Republic of Krajina. Some of them were in my possession, in view of the circumstances about which I informed the investigators, and some were in the bureau of the RSK's government in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to get that clear: The documents that were in the bureau of the RSK's government in Belgrade, were you able to use those for the purposes of preparation of your chronology?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some documents remained in my possession after March of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Mr. Babic. Please. Your answer -- your previous answer was: "Somewhere in the bureau of the RSK's government in Belgrade." So it is quite clear you are not there talking about documents in your possession; you are talking about documents which were somewhere else, in the bureau of the RSK's government in Belgrade. So what I was asking you was whether you were able to use those documents. Did you have access to those documents for the purposes of preparation of your chronology?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, yes, partially those documents from the bureau of the RSK's government which were left in my possession after May of 1996. That was the answer I gave previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, your answer was: "The documents I turned over to the Prosecution, the documents which were official documents from the archives pertaining to the Serbian Autonomous Region Krajina and Serbian Republic of Krajina, some of them were in my possession, in view of the circumstances about which I informed the investigators, and some were in the bureau of the RSK's government in Belgrade." Now, to be analytical about it, Mr. Babic, there are two classes of document there, those in your possession -- do you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Let me just correct. From the bureau of the government, that means that they were not located in that bureau but originated from that bureau. They were in my possession, and I had taken them from the government's bureau in Belgrade sometime in May of 1996. So both of these sets of documents were in my possession in late 2001. It's just that some originate from the archives in Knin and the others originate from the government's bureau in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I hope I make full allowance for the fact that being cross-examined is more stressful than doing the cross-examining. But I would, please, ask you to help the Trial Chamber, and me, incidentally as a secondary point at my cross-examination, by trying to be very careful about the questions and be as careful as you can about the answers? The --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Babic. So just to clear that up. Can we take it, then, that the only documents that you used for the preparation of this chronology were documents which were in fact in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were they all handed over to the -- well, whether it's the investigators or the Prosecution, and whether that's the same thing, were they all handed over to officials of this Tribunal, or offices.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The one that pertained to the topic of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, can we take it -- you say the ones that pertain to the topic of investigation. All the documents that you used for the -- in the preparation of your chronology?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These documents are the documents of the Assembly of Republic of Serbian Krajina, the government of the SAO Krajina, the Assembly of the SAO Krajina. There are a lot of those documents, decisions, appointments. A large number of documents. So these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you give the Trial Chamber some idea of the quantity of material that you're referring to? Dozens of pages? Hundreds of pages? Some broad indication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think more than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But less than 500?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there was a joint government session of the government of the SAO Krajina and the government of Republika Srpska, in Banja Luka, in October 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- I thought you had said, but maybe not - I ask you now - was there any sort of a meeting in Banja Luka relatively shortly before the meeting that you mention on the 23rd of October at the Federation Palace in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a meeting two days earlier, on the 20th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that meeting -- well, I'll put it in an open way to you, Mr. Babic. What was that meeting on the 20th of October? It was a meeting of whom, for what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, the meeting was held in the Federation Palace in Belgrade. It was officially called by the Presidency of Yugoslavia, based on my information. It had been scheduled pursuant to an instruction from Slobodan Milosevic, who attended only the beginning of the meeting. The media did not report him attending the meeting at all. And there were representatives of the Republic of Serbia attending, the socialist Republic of Serbia. No. I apologise. Republic of Serbia. The Republic of Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will interrupt you on this occasion, if I may. First of all, and I don't mean this question in the least bit offensively or it doesn't have some hidden meaning to it. Are you very tired at the moment, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. You speak about meetings, diaries. Then you come up with a meeting of the 20th in Banja Luka, the 23rd in Belgrade, and I have to shift mentally from the events on the 20th of October in Banja Luka without any warning from you to the events on the 23rd in Belgrade. This is why I have to prepare myself, both visually and mentally, to tell you about this. I'm not tired, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on questions and answers. You were asked, Mr. Babic, about a meeting that would have taken place shortly before the meeting of the 23rd of October. Could you tell us what the purpose of that meeting was and who attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand the question, Your Honour. I did not understand it just a few minutes ago because I thought the question was about the 23rd of October. So I apologise. The meeting on the 20th of October, 1991, in Banja Luka, was called by Dr. Karadzic. I was notified about the meeting by Slobodan Milosevic, who told me that I should attend it. I went to Banja Luka. There were representatives of the political leadership of Serbs in Bosnia Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and Herzegovina, Western Slavonia. I was there. I don't know whether there was anybody else from SAO Krajina there as well. It was a small gathering, perhaps 20 people. The meeting was called pursuant to The Hague Conference about the former Yugoslavia, and the purpose of the meeting was to have representatives of Serbs in Bosnia, Western Slavonia, and SAO Krajina give support to policies of the leadership of Serbia, as presented at The Hague Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did those 20 -- those 20 people, it would seem to follow, very clearly, on your evidence, would include Dr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He called the meeting. He chaired the meeting, gave a speech, promoted this gathering in the media, and this was more a media promotion of the meeting than a very significant meeting, in terms of its content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Significant enough, though, for Mr. Milosevic to have got in touch with you and say that you should attend?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for what reason did Mr. Milosevic -- what reason did Mr. Milosevic give you for you to attend?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to say that Mr. Milosevic has a very peculiar way of explaining things and expressing himself, so I have to say about two or three sentences about that, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's the Trial Chamber's permission, Mr. Babic, but so far as you need mine, with respect, you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that I was in Belgrade. I cannot remember exactly. After Milosevic's call, I came to his office very soon thereafter, after the meeting. When I came there, Mr. Milosevic was very angry. He was cursing Momir Bulatovic, rather, his mother. He called him a traitor, threatened him with Branko Kostic, and so on. That was after Mr. Bulatovic at The Hague Conference accepted the proposal of Mr. Carrington, the international facilitator, concerning the future of Yugoslavia. That was in contradiction of Milosevic's views at the conference. And after that, he told me that I need to go to Banja Luka, that Mr. Karadzic would explain to me there what is to be done, that we need to express support to Yugoslavia, and he even provided an aeroplane for me to travel from Belgrade to Banja Luka, as a result of which I arrived at Banja Luka that very day and I found Karadzic there. The meeting was held, and, as I said, this meeting was in fact a media promotion of the view taken by Milosevic at The Hague Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what was the -- there clearly was a difference of view. What was the divergence of view, then, between Mr. Milosevic -- well, first of all, who was Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the divergence of view between Mr. Bulatovic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, at the second Plenary Session of The Hague Conference, accepted the document on the future organisation of Yugoslavia, whereby it was envisioned that all those republics who seek independence will gain it. And there were three models of future relationships between these units. One was the federation, the second one was confederation, and the third option was independence. That was the content of that document. Milosevic supported the view that Yugoslavia needs to be continue on. He advocated the federation model, that option. This is briefly his position. Pragmatically-speaking, Milosevic was the only representative from Yugoslav republics who refused or declined to accept that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you have an indication from Mr. Milosevic in advance of the meeting when he contacted you of what Mr. Karadzic's position was in relation to that divergence between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it was well known. It was known to me as well, that Karadzic shared Milosevic's view. That was a well-known fact. I don't remember whether there was an actual discussion about it at the time, but the matter was completely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you go as the principal representative of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To the meeting in Banja Luka on the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a representative from Krajina, a representative of the government of the SAO Krajina. That was my role, my official role.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was Dr. Karadzic's official role?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, he was president of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and factually, he was one of the main leaders, political leaders, of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He was, effectively, the representative of Republika Srpska, wasn't he? I'm sorry. He was -- I beg your pardon. He was effectively the main, the principal representative of the Bosnian Serbs, as the, in effect equivalent of you, as the principal representative of the SAO Krajina government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this was not an official meeting where people had to appear in their official roles. There were a number of people there, not just main representatives. From Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was Dr. Karadzic, and also people from Banja Luka. So not all of the main leaders from Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was a small gathering, and it wasn't only the representatives exclusively who were there in their personal capacities. So I couldn't interpret it in the way that you depicted it, that I was the main representative from the SAO Krajina and that my counterpart from Bosnia was Dr. Karadzic. That's not how I would describe it. In my view, I believed it then and I believe it now, this was a gathering that was used to promote views, and it was attended by the people who frequently appeared in public in media. As I've said in the beginning, this was a media promotion of a political position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So how long did the meeting itself last?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. I don't think it lasted more than an hour. In my view, long enough to have TV cameras tape what was going on and to have the participants give statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were the press admitted to the meeting itself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Belgrade TV crew was there. There were also other television crews, but I cannot recall who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was there, Mr. Babic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I said that I don't recall him being there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if Mr. Krajisnik says he was there, can we take it that you wouldn't dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. I'll rephrase it. If Mr. Krajisnik says he was there, you know nothing whatever that would enable you to dispute that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing anything. I'm just telling you what I recall and what I know for sure. I don't understand the question. In what sense should I be disputing anything? I don't think it's up to me to dispute anything. I'm just telling you what I know and what I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, by contrast, a meeting that you say Mr. Krajisnik was present at on the 23rd of October, 1991, at the Federation Palace in Belgrade, is a meeting that Mr. Krajisnik says he was not present at.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was there in that capacity; namely, this was following the departure from the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly. I don't know whether the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina was already formed, but in that sense, he was representing the people, the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, when you say you remember that the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was there in that capacity, that's not exactly a coded expression, is it, Mr. Babic? The president of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic was -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was Mr. Krajisnik, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify something that I have already said. I know that Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik was the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the middle of the month, the Serb representatives left the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly and established the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I cannot remember what date this was established. At the time, in Belgrade, Mr. Krajisnik was one of the representatives of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the question simply is whether Mr. Krajisnik was present at that meeting in this palace on the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recollect, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've managed to convince my own team that I know what I'm talking about, Your Honour, so with that assurance I'm going to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, there was a session -- I say now I said I knew what I was talking about, but the -- there was the founding assembly of Republika Srpska on the 24th of October, 1991. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was called the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm sure that that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think you are correct about that, Mr. Babic. Thank you. I think you are correct about that at that point. But -- although that isn't in the end the substance of the question. So with that correction, and you seem to have a pretty good recollection, then, do you recall that there was the founding assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 24th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was held approximately at that time. I cannot recall the exact date. I think it was between the 13th and the 15th of October, 1991. The deputies of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina left the assembly, and within a short period of time, within seven to ten days, the Serbian Assembly -- the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'll put it to you and see whether you disagree, even if you may be uncertain about the dates. Do you know anything that would enable you to disagree with it was the 14th or 15th of October that the events involving the walking out of the Serb deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina occurred, and you are right, it was around ten days later, it was the 24th of October, 1991 that there was the first assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If I put it to you that those are the historical facts, do you know anything which enables you to say that that is wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just have given me a speech. I am not disputing historical facts. That is my answer. What I do know is that there was a period from when the Serb deputies of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina left the session of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, relating to the voting on the declaration of a sovereign or independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the cause. And this happened in October 1991. A few days after this event - I don't know if you mentioned the 24th, or I'm not disputing the date, I didn't provide a specific date - the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed. That is what I know about that event. You're asking me if I'm disputing historical facts. No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the practical difficulty for Mr. Krajisnik that, in preparation for the founding assembly of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina in -- on the 24th of October, 1991, on the 23rd of October, 1991, Mr. Krajisnik needed to be and was in fact in Sarajevo, preparing for that event? Does that jog your memory at all? Do you know anything at all about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any specific actions, but I know that the founding was something that was being prepared for. I don't know what Mr. Krajisnik was doing in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So leaving aside Mr. Krajisnik for the moment, who do you -- who else - let's put it that way - do you recall being at the meeting at the Federation Palace in Belgrade on the 23rd of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kostic, Borisav Jovic were there, Sejdo Bajramovic, the fourth member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia from Vojvodina. I will try to remember his name later. Then the president of the Assembly of Montenegro was also there, Slobodan Milosevic was there, Radovan Karadzic was there, Momcilo Krajisnik was there, Nikola Koljevic, Biljana Plavsic, Peko Dzakula, Goran Hadzic were also there, and some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you've re-asserted that Mr. Krajisnik was there, Mr. Babic. Are we taking it that whatever the historical facts, you have a clear recollection in your mind that Mr. Krajisnik was at that meeting on the 23rd of October, 1991, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that -- that meeting attended by the press?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that it was filmed for television, and I don't know who else from the media was there. The meeting was reported in the media. I also remember that the media did not report Slobodan Milosevic as being present. I don't know who they said was present, but I do remember that the media did not report Slobodan Milosevic as being present, even though he did attend the meeting. I don't recall the other things the media reported about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, just why do you draw attention to the fact that the media didn't report Mr. Milosevic as being present, even though he was? What's the -- why does that feature in your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was significant for me, and it made a strong impression on me personally, because I discussed something with Milosevic. I responded to his pressure that I should attend a meeting in Paris with international representatives regarding my statement for -- in favour of international representatives relating to The Hague Conference and The Hague documents. That was important for me. After that meeting I practically fled from Belgrade and I did not go to Paris because of the pressure from Milosevic. And later I saw a clip of that meeting saying that it was attended by the representatives from Bosnia, from SAO Krajina, from Herzegovina, from Montenegro. I cannot remember which people were said as to have chaired the meeting, and many of them were mentioned, except Milosevic. This was important to me. I simply had the impression that he wanted to conceal his presence, although he was the organiser of it all, in order for it to appear in public that the Serbs from Bosnia and Croatia, and the representatives of Montenegro and Serbia, who were not mentioned there, were disputing The Hague documents and supporting his policies on their own initiative, without his input. That was the conclusion. This was something that was obvious. And this is why this was important to me, and this is why I'm constantly referring to this occasion with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical as far as the Defence is concerned, Mr. Babic. If Mr. Krajisnik had been at that meeting, which you say he was, he would have, as far as you know, do you agree, he would have had neither the ability nor any motive to have the media conceal his attendance at the meeting? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really if I can comment on that. I assume that he wouldn't have a motive for that. I don't know. My answer is: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On the question of ability, then, you'd agree that Mr. Milosevic seems to be consistent with evidence you've given, Mr. Milosevic did have the ability to manipulate the media to that degree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, over his own media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the main -- if there was a main point, what was the main point of that meeting on the 23rd of October, 1991, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can draw the main point from Branko Kostic's conclusion after the meeting, and during the meeting, the main topic was to calculate the percentage of the population from the territories of the former Yugoslavia who were supporting Yugoslavia, the concept of the Federation, the policy promoted by Slobodan Milosevic. At the end of the meeting, Branko Kostic calculated that, based on the representatives of Serbs from Montenegro and from Bosnia and Herzegovina and from Croatia, something over 50 per cent of the population of Yugoslavia was in favour of Yugoslavia the way it was promoted or supported by Slobodan Milosevic. Perhaps we're talking about 52 per cent or something. I cannot remember the exact figure, but it was over 50 per cent. And this is something that Branko Kostic announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were there throughout the meeting, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say yes. I think so, yes. I cannot remember the way the meeting ended, but, according to what I remember, after it was finished, after the meeting was finished, I left Belgrade by a side route. But as far as I remember, I think that, yes, I was there until the end. It never occurred to me or I never thought that I left before the meeting was completed. I cannot specifically recall now the way the meeting was ended, when Kostic said that it was over and what we did and how we left. But I do recall his conclusion and the percentages, which means that that was at the end of the meeting. That's how I can tell that I stayed until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And could you then describe the process, as briefly as you can, but the process of the meeting by which percentage support from the populations of the different constituent elements of Yugoslavia were established by the particular representatives at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, based on the presence of the representatives themselves. It was noted that the president of the Assembly of Serbia, of Montenegro, and other officials of Serbia and Montenegro represented the entire republics of Serbia and Montenegro. It was noted that representatives of Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina represented all of the Serbian people from Bosnia and Herzegovina there. It was four of them. Perhaps there was somebody else. And it was noted that representatives of the SAO Krajina, of the SAO Western Slavonia and Eastern Slavonia and Baranja represent that entire region. So that is how we had the percentage of 52 per cent of the population in favour of Yugoslavia, according to that particular calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you personally convinced of the correctness of that calculated conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it could be correct, or approximately. I didn't really dwell on the particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kostic, the vice-president of the Presidency of the SFRY. At the time he was formally at the head of the rump Presidency of Yugoslavia, which was comprised of only four officials, four representatives of the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Four did not take part. So it was four members from the total of eight of the former Presidency of Yugoslavia who were disputed the right to represent the Yugoslavia by The Hague Conference. Kostic was the name of also the fourth representative from Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really have got to the point where, where I go next in this cross-examination is into an area where I am frankly not feeling equipped to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it take you to get there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, not today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not today?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a proposal to adjourn until Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has to be, because that is, with respect, that is the only -- that is the only logical conclusion. I cannot go further into the cross-examination today on that basis, so the answer must be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how much time you would need on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm likely to need something approaching a full day, Your Honour. It won't be just a -- it won't be just an hour or so. As Your Honour can see, we have the other meetings on that checklist, and Your Honour can see some of the other areas. So it can't be a short session. There's no question of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I indicated before, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber would take into consideration the -- well, we said the position at 4.00 this afternoon we would look at how the cross-examination was conducted. We have considered that, and we had already some discussion on the cross-examination during the last break. The Chamber grants you three more hours next Monday, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note what Your Honour has said. It's a pre-emptive decision. I note what Your Honour has said. I can do no more than note it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a decision, and if there's any need to change the decision, of course, if time comes, but until now, the Chamber was not impressed in the usual way it is by the efficiency of this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, rather not. I just gave -- I noted that some questions were put two, three times to the witness. His answers were often dealt with in a way which could have been more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only comment I wish to make is that I do not accept the stricture, with respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you do not agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. Respectfully, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there -- since you might be then surprised that we would adjourn until next Monday, is there anything still to be discussed at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, nothing that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is there anything else on the agenda which you would need to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Babic, this means that we'll continue next Monday, and I'm looking at you, Madam Registrar, whether it would be in the same courtroom. I note that it's at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then be in Courtroom II next Monday, and we'll adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of June 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
